places.seoDescription: Siliguri: Bagdogra airport and New Jalpaiguri station, the Toy Train, Coronation Bridge, Bengal Safari Park and Salugara Monastery. Gateway to the hills.

overview.text:
Siliguri sits where the Himalayas rise out of the plains, on the Mahananda river, and it is the gateway for almost every trip to Darjeeling, Sikkim and the Dooars. Its name refers to the pebbles that once lined the riverbanks; today it is a busy city known for its '3 Ts' — tea, timber and tourism.

Most visitors pass through, but it repays a day: ride the Toy Train, see the Coronation Bridge over the Teesta, visit the Bengal Safari Park and the 100-ft stupa of the Salugara Monastery, and eat sel roti, thukpa and phaley before heading up into the hills.

overview.text:
Kurseong sits at about 1,483 m on the road and railway between Siliguri and Darjeeling — 34 km from the first and 32 km from the second. It is smaller and calmer than Darjeeling, wrapped in tea gardens, and has a pleasant climate through the year; the British prized it for its cool, dry summers.

Come for the tea: Makaibari, one of the oldest estates, still works the old way. Walk the forest trails and waterfalls around town or trek down towards the Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary, and visit the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Museum in his brother's house at Giddhapahar.

overview.text:
Lava — also written Labha — is a small Himalayan village in Kalimpong district, all wooden homes, crafts and forest. It sits right beside Neora Valley National Park, and its trails climb through rhododendron and fir past moss-covered rocks and birdsong. In winter it is said to be the only place in West Bengal that gets snow.

Stay with a local family, sip butter tea, and time your visit for the Sky Lantern Festival if you can. Lolegaon, with its Canopy Walk and Kanchenjunga views, is about 22 km away, and Changey Falls is close by.

how_to_reach.text: Fly to Bagdogra or take a train to New Jalpaiguri, then continue by road into the Kalimpong hills.

best_time.text: Lava is lovely in warm weather and at its most magical in winter, when it may get snow.

overview.text:
Lolegaon (Loleygaon) is a quiet village at about 1,675 m in the Kalimpong hills, 24 km from Lava. A short walk to Kafer, about 1 km away, gives a panoramic view of Kanchenjunga, and the village is wrapped in dense forest with waterfalls, old monasteries and plenty of birds and butterflies.

It is about a four-hour drive from Siliguri. Eat simply — momos, thukpa and gundruk soup with a cup of Darjeeling tea.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Siliguri via Kalimpong and Lava — about 124 km and four hours. Buses and taxis also run.

The park closes for the monsoon from 16 June to 15 September; come between November and March. Around it lie Dooars tea gardens and the hill villages of Samsing and Suntalekhola, and most visitors stay at Lataguri or Ramsai.

Jaldapara spreads across about 217 sq km of tall grassland and riverine forest on the Torsa river in Alipurduar district. Next door, Chilapata forest forms the corridor that elephants and rhinos use between Jaldapara and Buxa.

places.name: Bishnupur

places.seoTitle: Bishnupur — terracotta temples of the Mallas

overview.text:
Bishnupur, in Bankura district, was the capital of the Malla kings, and it is Bengal's great terracotta town. Stone was scarce, so builders turned to burnt brick, and in the 17th century the craft reached its peak: Raja Jagat Malla and his descendants raised temple after temple covered in terracotta panels.

Rasmancha, built by King Hambir in 1600, is the oldest brick temple; the five-pinnacled Shyam Rai (1643) and the twin-roofed Jore-Bangla are the showpieces. Bishnupur is also famous for Baluchari saris and its own gharana of Hindustani classical music, and the Bishnupur fair fills the town each December.

how_to_reach.text: Regular trains run from Kolkata to Bishnupur; Kolkata airport is about 212 km from Bankura.

overview.text:
Murshidabad was the capital of the Nawabs of Bengal. Murshid Quli Khan founded it and named it after himself, and through the 18th century it was a rich, cosmopolitan city where merchant families and companies kept their head offices.

Its landmark is Hazarduari Palace, built in 1824–1838 for Nawab Humayun Jah to designs by Colonel Duncan McLeod — three storeys in Italianate style on a 17-hectare site, with a library holding a hand-written Quran about 1.2 m long. Siraj-ud-Daulah's palace stood by the Motijhil, and the battlefield of Plassey, where he lost Bengal in 1757, is at Palashi to the south.
